newsitem.title: INDIA: India opposition welcomes water pact with caution.
newsitem.headline: India opposition welcomes water pact with caution.

text.p: India's leading opposition parties cautiously welcomed a treaty signed on Thursday with Bangladesh on the sharing of disputed Ganges River water, and left themselves room to later criticise its details.

"Any step that improves relations with Bangladesh must be welcomed," Atal Behari Vajpayee, leader of the opposition Hindu nationalist Bharaitya Janata Party (BJP), said in parliament of the 30-year accord.
But he said he could not comment on the details of the treaty until his party considered them carefully.
"We can talk about the accord only after reading the (detailed) statement," Vajpayee said shortly after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda announced the treaty.

Deve Gowda and visiting Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina signed the treaty that guarantees a minimum water flow of 35,000 cusecs (cubic feet per second) to Bangladesh from the Farakka Barrage when the flow there is 70,000 cusecs or more.
When the flow falls below 70,000 cusecs, as it usually does between March and May every year, the two countries would share the water equally, Deve Gowda said.

A decades-old dispute worsened in 1974 when India built the Farakka Barrage 18 km (11 miles) from the border where the river crosses into Bangladesh. Dhaka later accused India of exposing Bangladesh to gradual desertification by holding back water.
In 1977, India agreed to guarantee a minimum flow of 34,000 cusecs from the Ganges to Bangladsh, but dropped the move during a review five years later.
Some Indian opposition leaders say the accord, crucial to Hasina's political future, is a concession to Bangladesh.

"It (the treaty) will create a milestone in the history of our bilateral relations," Priya Ranjan Das Munshi of the Congress party told parliament. But he added that the government must take steps to safeguard the interests of the nation.
Das Munshi is a lawmaker from West Bengal, the eastern Indian state whose Calcutta port needs Ganges water.

"This is an accord we should heartily welcome," said Somnath Chatterjee, leader of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), which heads the West Bengal state government. CPI-M was a key party involved in negotiating the treaty.
Hasina was scheduled to leave for Dhaka later on Thursday after a three-day visit.
